source.title: Detection of Printed Circuit Board Defects on ENIG and ENIPIG Surface Finishes with Convolutional Neural Networks and Evaluation of Training Parameters
source.authors: Angelika Hable; Paul Tabatabai; H. L. Lichtenegger; Anton Scherr; T. Krivec; D. Gruber

record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps batch size and learning rate under a fixed epoch count and evaluates held-out performance, using PCB defect-detection metrics rather than the generalization-gap measures in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports batch-size trends in figures and explicitly states the F1-score maxima and the best tested setting. Pretraining, augmentation, and the single fixed epoch count are part of the setup; the paper does not report random-label fitting or training error.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out defect-detection performance while varying batch size at a fixed eight-epoch budget. This tests V5 in a new setting: pretrained ResNet18 on PCB images.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: relatively low batch size and learning rate produced the best tested results, with maximum F1 of 93.9% at batch 16 and learning rate 10^-4. Dataset dependence is the authors' interpretation, rather than a controlled comparison across datasets.
record.recipe_differences: Pretrained ResNet18, PCB defect classification with image augmentation and a 1cycle Adam training policy; evaluates test TPR, TNR, and F1-score rather than train-test error gap.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size and learning rate alter TPR, TNR, and F1-score; the TPR/TNR extrema differ by learning rate, and the best F1-score occurs at different batch sizes for the two learning rates.
record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Microelectronics and Electronic Packaging, 2022
record.problems: Only one architecture and PCB task are evaluated. Training error is not reported, so the train-test gap cannot be assessed directly. The held-out set contains 150 PCB images from sample 2, and the incompletely filled vias class is absent from that set. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No required results omitted. The paper's average defect detections per defect are not a generalization measure named by V5 and do not directly measure the batch-size effect on held-out performance.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width-dependent generalization beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD comparisons and tuning-dependent differences.

Language models, longer training, controlled tests of warmup, normalization or regularization changes, and systematic identification of a batch-size threshold. Learning-rate scaling receives only a qualitative cross-setting comparison.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Measured magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removal of memorized training examples versus random removal.

missing.what: Comparative F1 results across batch sizes at each learning rate, including the larger-batch values relative to the reported maxima. The supplied text establishes the qualitative preference for smaller batches but does not supply numerical penalties.

The authors report similar F1 for learning rate 10^-3 with batch 512 and learning rate 10^-4 with batches 32 or 64. Record this qualitative cross-recipe comparison, without treating it as proof that scaling eliminates the small-batch penalty.
missing.locator: Results and Discussion, p. 129, paragraph immediately before Conclusions.

missing.what: Precision is stated to fall with increasing batch size, explaining why F1 peaks before recall. This helps interpret the opposing recall and specificity trends.
missing.locator: Results and Discussion, p. 128, discussion of Fig. 8.

record.verdict_notes: Non-monotonic recall and specificity do not by themselves limit V5, which already allows a workload-dependent threshold. One network was trained per setting, with no reported uncertainty. Sharpness is discussed through cited work rather than measured, so it supplies no V7 evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test performance coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the interpolation threshold.
CNN versus fully connected comparisons and local-connectivity effects.
Adaptive optimizer versus SGD held-out comparisons.

The study tests a single pretrained ResNet18 on PCB defect detection at eight epochs; it does not test language models, workload-dependent batch thresholds, longer training, or the recipe adaptations listed in the version.
Dropout intervention and its interaction with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the change in test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.stage_stated: pretrained on ImageNet 2012; trained for eight epochs on PCB image patches
rows.operation_detail: Trained with batch-size sweep and maximum learning rate 10^-3; 1cycle policy; test F1-score evaluated
rows.measure: F1-score on the PCB test dataset
rows.locator: Results and Discussion; Fig. 8(a) and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper says the best evaluation results were achieved at lower batch sizes and learning rates; this is the reported maximum for this learning rate.
rows.check: The 93.6% F1 maximum at batch size 64 is correct, but it is a selected optimum without a larger-batch comparator. Replace or supplement this selection row with the within-learning-rate F1 comparison. The text explicitly reports that smaller batches performed best.

rows.check: The 93.9% F1 maximum at batch size 16 is correct, but this selected optimum alone does not measure a batch-size penalty. Add the larger-batch F1 comparison at the same learning rate.

rows.note: Text states that TPR rises with batch size to a maximum and then falls; the maximum is at batch size 512 for this learning rate. No plotted values transcribed.
rows.check: Recall increases through batch size 512 and then decreases. This is a mixed-direction sweep, not a uniformly adverse large-batch effect. Split the increasing and decreasing portions; numerical effect sizes are unavailable in the supplied text.

relationships.condition: Pretrained ResNet18, PCB defect detection, eight epochs, maximum learning rates 10^-3 and 10^-4; aggregate F1 performance.
relationships.reason: The text explicitly states that smaller batches performed best; R1 and R2 locate the F1 maxima at batches 64 and 16. This verdict rests on the comparative text missing from those selection rows; the penalty's magnitude is unavailable.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports higher F1 with smaller batches, but this result has not been verified. The size of the advantage was unavailable.
